marks.gloss_en: ומי סבר ליה כוותיה? והא מפליג פליג עליה, דתניא: ... אמר לו רבי יהודה: והלא מן התורה הוא אסור -- R' Yehuda's retort shows he and RYBZ disagree
the baraita: RYBZ enacted the whole-day prohibition; R' Yehuda said to him: is it not forbidden by Torah law? (gloss-only: the exchange's force -- that they disagree -- is carried by obj_mifliag)
רבי יהודה הוא דקא טעי, הוא סבר מדרבנן קאמר, ולא היא, מדאורייתא קאמר (reified as p_ribaz_deoraita, which 41b.3 goes on to attack)
והא ״התקין״ קאמר! -- but [the mishna/baraita] says 'enacted', which marks a rabbinic enactment
מאי התקין -- דרש והתקין (= p_darash_vehitkin)
[R' Yehuda] thought RYBZ was speaking of a rabbinic prohibition
as it is written, 'until this very day'
R' Yosei: if the first festival day fell on Shabbat and he forgot and carried the lulav out to the public domain, he is exempt
כי הא דאמר רבא: הא לך אתרוג זה על מנת שתחזירהו לי... החזירו יצא -- a gift on condition of return serves for the mitzva
Rava: 'here is this etrog on condition that you return it to me' -- he took it and fulfilled with it: if he returned it, he fulfilled

מיתיבי: לא יאחז אדם תפילין בידו וספר תורה בחיקו ויתפלל... ואמר שמואל: סכין וקערה ככר ומעות הרי אלו כיוצא בהן -- holding objects while praying is forbidden, so how could Ameimar pray holding the lulav?
Mar bar Ameimar: my father would pray with it [the lulav in hand]
התם לאו מצוה נינהו וטריד בהו, הכא מצוה נינהו ולא טריד בהו -- there they are not a mitzva and he is preoccupied with them; here it is a mitzva and he is not preoccupied
Shmuel: a knife, a bowl, a loaf and coins are like them
'and you shall take' -- that the taking be in the hand of each and every one
the maaseh: RG, R' Yehoshua, R' Elazar ben Azarya and R' Akiva on a ship, only RG having a lulav; each took it, fulfilled with it, and gave it to the next as a gift
a gift on condition of return is called a gift
to tell you how beloved the mitzvot were to them
R' Elazar bar Tzadok: the custom of the people of Jerusalem -- the lulav in hand leaving home, going to synagogue, reciting Shema and praying, visiting the sick and comforting mourners
to tell you how zealous they were in mitzvot
